Private Showing

200 Hollycrest Drive  ·  Pinehurst, North Carolina  ·  Est. 1916

Garran Hill

Neo-Georgian  ·  Walter Hines Page  ·  Built 1916

The Estate  ·  Neo-Georgian

Some houses hold history.
This one shaped it.

Ordered by Walter Hines Page in 1913. Completed by Leonard Tufts' craftsmen in 1916.

Flemish bond brick. A brick water table at the foundation. White portico. Paired chimneys. A circular lawn held before the entrance like a pause.

Garran Hill  ·  1916

The door has been open since 1916.

Seven fireplaces. Four columns. Original 1916 brick. 4.15 acres. 6,072 square feet.

It has not been divided. It has not been converted. It has not been asked to be something else.

The History  ·  Walter Hines Page

He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

He bought the land in February 1913. Named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James.

He sailed for London. Into the war.

The house was completed without him. His son Ralph supervised. Leonard Tufts' craftsmen built it. From London, through four years of war, he wrote home about one thing.

“The farm — the farm — the farm.” The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page  ·  Vol. I, P. 354  ·  1923

He came home in December 1918. Carried from the train at Aberdeen. He died ten days later.

He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Co. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. He nominated Woodrow Wilson for the presidency.

He never spent a night here.

Source: PineStraw Magazine “A Page Out of History” · October 2019

“Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn’t I?”

Walter Hines Page  ·  Aberdeen, NC  ·  December 1918 He died ten days later.

As Seen In

“What Ambassador Walter Hines Page started, others have continued in a style both innovative and respectful of times when people paid calls, wrote thank-you notes and took Sunday drives.”

PineStraw Magazine  ·  October 2019

The Threshold

The staircase has turned the same curve since 1916.

Mahogany volute. Original leaded glass. Herringbone brick underfoot. Arched fanlights overhead.

The Library

Three walls of shelving.
A rolling ladder.

French doors to the garden. The kind of room that makes you want to stay.

The Rooms

Georgian mantel. Delft tile.
Original shell cabinets.

The drawing room holds a Georgian mantel with original Delft tile surround. The dining room: shell cabinets, original 1916 plasterwork, intact.

The Kitchen

White cabinetry. Dark granite.
Heart pine underfoot.

Island. Four windows. Room to cook. Heart-pine floors — the only room in the house that holds them.

The Grounds  ·  4.15 Acres

In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.

The world outside these gates does not exist here.

Salt water pool, 20×40 ft. Installed 2022. Four acres of hardwood canopy.

“Someone still puts flowers there.”

Blue Fox  ·  Betty Dumaine’s horse  ·  buried on the grounds 1959 – 1984

The Restoration  ·  1999–2001

Thomas O’Shea.
Two years. Done right.

General contractor Dennis Dunagan. The original materials were preserved where possible. The intention was stewardship, not renovation.

Seven fireplaces, six on propane. Oak floors throughout. The mahogany staircase untouched.

Garran Hill

Garran Hill is ready.
It is offered now for the first time.
